items.stem: Which comes closest to how federal income tax rates should be set?
items.scope: Think about the overall system, not your own tax bill.
items.context: Today there are seven federal income tax rates, from 10% on the first part of taxable income to 37% on income above about $640,000 for a single person.
options: Much more graduated than today, with a top rate above 50% on the highest incomes
Somewhat more graduated: higher rates on the highest incomes, the same or lower on middle incomes
Keep today's structure of rates from 10% to 37%
Fewer rates and a lower top rate, such as two or three rates between 10% and 30%
One flat rate for everyone on income above a basic tax-free amount
No federal income tax; raise the money another way, such as a national sales tax

facts.claim: Seven brackets, 10% to 37%; 37% bracket starts above $640,600 (single) for tax year 2026
facts.source: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32; KPMG TaxNewsFlash summary (Oct 2025)

definitions.text: Higher rates apply to each additional slice of income as income rises. A rate applies only to the income in its bracket, not to all of a person's income.

items.stem: Which comes closest to your view on federal income tax for households with low incomes?
items.scope: Federal income tax only. Payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare are separate.
items.context: In a typical year about 4 in 10 households owe no federal income tax, often because of credits for children and low-wage work.
options: Owe nothing, and get larger refundable credits than today
Owe nothing, with about today's refundable credits
Owe nothing, but with smaller refundable credits than today
Pay a small minimum income tax, such as $100 a year
Pay the same flat rate as everyone else, with no tax-free amount

facts.claim: Roughly 40% of US households owe no federal income tax in a typical year
facts.source: Tax Policy Center, 'Who doesn't pay federal income tax?' (annual estimates)

definitions.text: Tax credits that can be paid out as a refund even if a household owes no income tax, such as the Earned Income Tax Credit.

items.stem: In principle, how should the tax burden be shared between people with high and low incomes?
items.scope: Count all the taxes a person pays, not only income tax.
options: People with high incomes should pay a much larger share of their income in taxes
People with high incomes should pay a somewhat larger share of their income
Everyone should pay the same share of their income above a basic tax-free amount
Everyone should pay the same share of all their income, with no tax-free amount

items.stem: What should the federal income tax rate be on each dollar a person earns above $1 million a year?
items.scope: This is the rate on income above $1 million only, not on all of that person's income.
options: 70% or higher
About 50% to 60%
About 40% to 45%
37%, as today
About 25% to 30%
20% or lower

facts.claim: Top federal individual income tax rate is 37%, made permanent by Public Law 119-21 (July 2025)

items.stem: What should the federal tax rate on corporate profits be?
items.scope: Think about profitable companies in general, large and small.
items.context: The rate has been 21% since 2018. Before that it was 35%.
options: 35% or higher
About 28%
21%, as today
About 15%

facts.claim: Federal corporate rate cut from 35% (top bracket) to a flat 21% starting 2018
facts.source: Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, Public Law 115-97

items.subtopic: Wealth tax on very large fortunes
items.stem: Should the federal government tax the total wealth of the very richest households each year?
items.scope: Assume the tax applies only to wealth above $50 million, a tiny fraction of households.
options: Yes, 3% or more a year on wealth above $50 million
Yes, about 1% to 2% a year
No yearly wealth tax, but tax large gains in value when wealth is passed on at death
No; tax income, not wealth

definitions.text: Everything a household owns, such as stocks, businesses, real estate and savings, minus its debts.

facts.claim: Households with net worth above $50 million are roughly 0.05%-0.1% of US households
facts.source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances; Saez & Zucman wealth tax estimates
facts.note: Scope now says 'a tiny fraction' instead of an unverified count.

items.subtopic: Wealth tax on very large fortunes
items.stem: Which comes closest to your view of very large fortunes, such as $1 billion or more?
items.scope: Think about how taxes should treat them, not about any particular person.
options: They are a problem in themselves; taxes should be set to shrink them over time
The richest should pay much more in taxes than now
The richest should pay somewhat more than now
The richest pay about the right amount now
Taxes on the richest are already too high and discourage investment

items.stem: What should happen to the federal tax on large estates passed on at death?
items.scope: This tax is paid out of the estate, before heirs receive it.
items.context: Today it applies only to the part of an estate above $15 million per person, at a 40% rate. Fewer than 1 in 1,000 estates owe it.
options: Apply it to estates above about $1 million, with rates of 50% or more on the largest
Apply it to estates above about $3.5 million (the 2009 level), at about 45%
Keep today's rules
Raise the threshold so even fewer estates pay
Eliminate the estate tax

facts.claim: Basic exclusion amount $15 million per person for 2026, indexed after; top rate 40%
facts.source: Public Law 119-21 (2025); IRS estate tax page

facts.claim: Fewer than 0.1% of estates owe federal estate tax
facts.source: Joint Committee on Taxation; Tax Policy Center estimates

items.stem: Which comes closest to your view of taxing very large inheritances?
items.scope: Think about inheritances of several million dollars or more, not ordinary family savings.
options: A large share should go to the public, so wealth doesn't build up across generations
A moderate tax on them is fair
Only a small tax, on the very largest
No tax at all; the money was already taxed when it was earned

items.stem: How should profits from selling investments, such as stocks, be taxed compared with wages?
items.scope: Think about investments held for more than a year.
items.context: Today these profits are taxed at up to 20% (plus a 3.8% surtax on high earners). Wages are taxed at up to 37%.
options: The same rates as wages for everyone
The same rates as wages for people with high incomes; lower rates for everyone else
Lower rates than wages, as today
Lower rates than today
Not taxed at all

facts.claim: Long-term capital gains rates 0/15/20%; 3.8% net investment income tax above $200k single / $250k joint

items.stem: Stock bought for $100,000 is worth $1 million when its owner dies. Under today's rules, the $900,000 gain is never taxed as income. What should happen?
items.scope: Think about large estates. Family farms and small businesses could get special treatment under any option.
options: Tax those gains at death, above an exemption of about $1 million
Don't tax at death, but heirs pay tax on the full gain when they sell
Keep today's rule: heirs pay tax only on gains after they inherit

facts.claim: Inherited assets receive a basis equal to fair market value at death ('step-up'), so pre-death gains escape income tax

items.stem: Which comes closest to what government should do about cash and food aid for low-income households?
items.scope: Programs like food stamps (SNAP), the Earned Income Tax Credit and cash welfare. Health coverage is asked separately.
options: Guarantee every household enough to stay above the poverty line
Spend more than today, mainly for families with children and people who can't work
Keep spending at about today's level
Spend less than today; more help should come from charities, churches and families
End most federal cash and food aid; leave it to states, charities and families

items.stem: How much say should people getting aid have over how they spend it?
items.scope: Think about aid for basic needs such as food and housing.
options: Mostly cash; people decide for themselves how to spend it
A mix of cash and benefits for specific needs, as today
Mostly benefits for specific needs, like food and rent, so money goes to essentials
Benefits for specific needs, with limits on what can be bought, such as no soda or candy with food aid

items.stem: Should adults who can work have to work, look for work, or train in order to get cash or food aid?
items.scope: Think of adults aged 18 to 54 with no disability and no children at home. You'll be able to add exceptions next.
options: No; aid should not depend on work
No requirement, but offer job training and help finding work
Yes, about 20 hours a week of work, job search or training, after a grace period of about 3 months
Yes, 30 or more hours a week from the start, and benefits end for anyone who doesn't comply

items.stem: Should each of these people also have to meet the work requirement you chose?
items.scope: Answer each case separately.
options: Should be exempt
Should have to meet it

cases.text: Parents whose youngest child is 6 to 13 years old
People caring full-time for a disabled family member
People living in an area with very high unemployment

items.stem: Should the federal government send every adult a regular cash payment, regardless of income or whether they work?
items.scope: Assume taxes would rise to pay for any payment.
options: Yes, enough to live on: about $1,500 a month or more
Yes, a smaller payment of about $500 a month
No universal payment, but a guaranteed minimum income for anyone below a set level
No guaranteed income of any kind

definitions.text: Often called universal basic income: the same amount sent to every adult, with no work requirement and no income test.

items.stem: Which comes closest to the federal support you want for families with children?
items.scope: Think about support through the tax code or direct payments.
items.context: Today parents can get a tax credit of up to $2,200 per child. Families with low earnings get only part of it.
options: A monthly payment of about $300 for every child, whatever the parents' income
A larger credit than today, with the full amount for low-income families
Keep about today's credit
A smaller credit, only for families who owe income tax
No federal child credit

facts.claim: Child Tax Credit $2,200 per child from tax year 2025, indexed for inflation; refundable portion limited and requires earned income

items.stem: Should parents with no earnings from work get the full child tax credit?
items.scope: Think of parents who are not disabled and not retired.
options: Yes, the full amount, whether or not they work
A partial amount
No; only parents with earnings from work should get it

items.subtopic: Inequality as a problem for government
items.stem: Which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Think about the gap between the richest and everyone else in the US.

sides.label: Reduce the gap
sides.text: Government should act to reduce the gap between rich and poor, even if that means higher taxes and slower growth.

sides.label: Focus on growth
sides.text: Government should focus on growth and not try to reduce the gap, even if it gets wider.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.stem: The federal government spends much more than it collects in taxes. Which comes closest to what should be done?
items.scope: Think about the next ten years.
items.context: In 2025 the federal government spent about $1.8 trillion more than it collected.
options: Borrowing is fine for now; focus on other priorities
Close the gap mainly by raising taxes on high earners and corporations
Close the gap with an even mix of tax increases and spending cuts
Close the gap mainly by cutting spending
Close the gap entirely by cutting spending, with no tax increases

facts.source: Congressional Budget Office, Monthly Budget Review (Oct 2025)

items.notes: Option 0 is held on both left (spend now) and right (cut taxes now); expect a non-monotone curve and check with the nominal model.

items.stem: Should the Constitution require the federal government to balance its budget every year?
items.scope: Spending could not exceed tax revenue in a year.
options: No; the government needs to be able to borrow
Only in normal times, with exceptions for wars and recessions
Yes, every year, with no exceptions

items.stem: When people in the US are poor, what is usually the main reason?
items.scope: Think about working-age adults without disabilities.
options: An economic system that is unfair to them
Circumstances they didn't choose, like where they grew up or bad luck
A mix of their circumstances and their own choices
Their own choices, like dropping out of school or not working
Lack of effort

items.stem: Should the federal government guarantee a job to anyone who wants to work but can't find one?
items.scope: Public jobs such as care work or infrastructure, paid at least the minimum wage.
options: Yes, for anyone who wants one
Only in areas with high unemployment
No; help with job searches and training instead
No; jobs should come from the private sector

items.stem: Should income from tips and overtime pay be taxed the same as other wages?
items.scope: Federal income tax only.
options: Yes, all income should be taxed the same way
Exempt it only for workers with low or middle incomes
Exempt it for everyone
items.notes: Popular across parties; a POP candidate as much as REDIS.
